Executive Summary This work shows that two strategies—(1) improved forecasting of price-responsive electric vehicle (EV) charging and (2) flattening EV charging price-response over similarly priced times—can greatly increase the percentage of personal light-duty vehicles that can participate in time-of-use or real-time price electric vehicle managed charging (EVMC) and by so doing contribute to bulk power system cost reductions. Furthermore, the outcomes for price-responsive EVMC can be similar to or exceed those of direct load control (DLC) up to high participation levels, especially when charging is scheduled within single sessions using coarse price signals (time-of-use rates). Light-duty vehicle EVMC, whether price-responsive or DLC, can reduce power system costs by better aligning EV charging with locations and times of low energy cost or infrastructure use. Coordinating charging across thousands to millions of electric vehicles while preserving mobility service is a barrier to realizing the value of EVMC. Price-responsive dispatch mechanisms like time-of-use rates and real-time prices can be attractive compared to DLC because they only require one-way communications and can schedule individual vehicle charging with full knowledge of both flexibility and price. However, increasing participation in price-responsive mechanisms is known to induce costly electricity consumption spikes when many EVs respond to the same price signal at the same time. We quantify the ability of improved EVMC forecasting to sustain savings from price-responsive mechanisms beyond the limits observed in previous work of 4% to 14% of light-duty vehicles participating (Hale et al. 2022a). Perfect forecasting of price-responsive EV load makes time-of- use and real-time price bulk power system production cost savings similar to those of DLC with up to 27% to 45% or more light-duty vehicles
